title: When Routes Run Out: Adversarial Co-Learning and Explainable Robustness in Quantum Repeater Networks
authors: Brennan Bell, Inti Gabriel Mendoza Estrada, Andreas Trügler, Paul Erker
abstract: We study an adversarial bandit problem for entanglement-based quantum-network routing over a modest graph corpus. Alice selects an end-to-end repeater route for an Ekert-91 protocol (E91) representing her move, while Eve selects an attack surface, either edge intercept--resend or repeater memory degradation. Payoffs are drawn from cached SeQUeNCe-simulated E91 transcripts, and Alice accepts a turn when the finite-sample statistic violates the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) bound. Performing adversarial co-learning across 50 structured topologies, we find that learned retention tracks a full-matrix minimax reference closely (Pearson $r=0.99$): under a one-surface Eve action model, bottleneck families have zero retention, while non-bottleneck families follow a $1-1/N$ coverage principle. We then fit decision-tree explanation models to graph-, attack-, and route-level topology-corpus targets and report their faithfulness. Finally, we construct prompt records for local language models to summarize the tree evidence, resulting in an open-source explanation workflow for quantum-repeater network games.
summary: This paper models quantum repeater network routing as an adversarial game where an attacker (Eve) tries to degrade entanglement links while a sender (Alice) chooses routes. By using advanced co-learning algorithms and analyzing the resulting strategies, the authors demonstrate that network bottlenecks are critical vulnerabilities, providing both quantitative robustness measures and explainable insights into these weaknesses.
main_problem: The study investigates adversarial robustness in quantum-network routing when resources (routes) are limited, framed as an adversarial bandit problem.
main_result: Adversarial co-learning successfully recovers the minimax strategy structure, showing that network bottlenecks lead to zero retention while non-bottleneck paths follow a predictable $1 - 1/N$ coverage principle.
method: The authors employ adversarial co-learning (Exp3) against simulated quantum communication transcripts and use decision-tree regressors followed by LLMs for explainability analysis.
model_or_system: The model is an entanglement-based quantum repeater network utilizing the Ekert-91 (E91) protocol. The game involves Alice selecting a route and Eve choosing an attack surface (edge intercept–resend or memory degradation).
key_observables: CHSH violation ($|S|$), learned retention rate, Nash equilibrium gap decay, and decision-tree faithfulness ($R^2$).
important_parameters: 50 structured topologies across eight structural families; the CHSH bound ($	ext{S} > 2$); finite sample size for learning.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that learned strategies can approximate the full-matrix minimax reference, and that LLMs can be prompted to summarize complex decision evidence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate exemplary topologies (bottleneck vs. disjoint), compare theoretical oracle retention ($1 - 1/N$) against observed learning results, and show probability mass distributions of learned strategies for Alice and Eve.
paper_structure: The paper first sets up the adversarial bandit game on quantum repeaters using E91 transcripts. It then applies adversarial co-learning to measure robustness across various topologies. Finally, it develops an open-source explanation workflow by fitting decision trees to map topology features to strategic outcomes and summarizing these findings with LLMs.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for testing the resilience of quantum communication protocols against sophisticated, adaptive adversaries, which is crucial for designing practical quantum internet infrastructure.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Exemplar topologies. (a) In a single-bottleneck graph every route crosses one node (red): Eve can deny all traffic from one surface. (b) In a disjoint-parallel graph one attack surface covers only one of N routes.
Fig. 2. Oracle retention versus node-disjoint path count N for all 50 topologies (log2 axis; coincident points jittered). Non-bottleneck families track 1 −1/N; bottleneck families sit at zero.

Fig. 3. Learned (time-averaged) Exp3 strategies aggregated by family. (a) Eve’s probability mass by action type. (b) Alice’s mass by route rank (routes sorted by learned probability per graph; “9+” sums the tail). Cell labels give the mean mass.
Fig. 4. Nash-gap decay across all 50 topologies (gray: individual graphs; blue: median and 10–90% band). The median halves between 105 and 5×105 turns.

Fig. 5. Mean scores for local LLMs (columns). Rubric (rows) evaluation over 50 scored prompt responses per LLM. Rubric criteria: numeric faithfulness (do stated numbers appear verbatim in the prompt), scope honesty (no security or physical-validity over-claims), decision tree referencing (does it refer to the correct tree leaf for its graph), and section completeness (how many of the requested sections are in the response), are automatically verified. The subjective, human interpretability score was evaluated by the authors and cross-referenced against Claude Fable 5 [21] in an independent blind pass.
